rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined about what is and is not pitchable. Its line, "Do not pitch this without the filings check — the whole angle collapses if the number is disclosed somewhere," is the adult supervision this update needs. B has good bones, but "Toast wants to be its restaurants' bank" stretches the supplied facts into a bigger claim than the proof can carry.
gaps_in_A: "Toast reached profitability by selling loans, not hardware" is sharper than the facts allow; the body correctly softens it into a margin-mix question, but the headline implies causation not yet proven.
"an industry with well-known failure rates" imports outside context. It may be true, but it was not in the update and belongs in required proof, not the angle's premise.

Several angles are gated by filings and Toast-side details: "size of the Toast Capital book," "segment-level revenue," and "credit-loss line item." That is rigorous, but it means pitchability is still conditional.
gaps_in_B: "Toast wants to be its restaurants' bank" and "The restaurant POS is becoming the restaurant's bank" overstate the update. Cash advances plus payroll do not automatically equal banking.
"documented fee complaints" upgrades the supplied fact. The update says some owners complained; it does not say the complaints are documented, material, or tied to lending.
"tip distribution, shifting hours, and high turnover" adds plausible restaurant-payroll context, but only tipped and hourly staff were supplied. Plausible is still not proof.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," comes too early. This set needs a current peg and a default-rate or filings check before anyone starts picking reporters.
